newsitem.title: USA: Dollar lower after German banker's remarks lift mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar lower after German banker's remarks lift mark.

text.p: The dollar fell sharply Tuesday, hurt when the mark rallied across the board after a German central banker spoke of a postponement in Europe's planned currency union.

The mark extended recent gains against the pound and several of its European counterparts after Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher joined a number of German officials who this week seemed to throw cold water on the plan to merge Europe's currencies in 1999.

"It's a broad-based dollar sale, in combination with a broad-based advance of the deutschemark against its major trading partners," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.
On Tuesday, the dollar fell to 1.6730 marks from 1.6910 on Monday. It also declined to 122.43 yen from 123.74 yen and to 1.4385 Swiss francs from 1.4590 Swiss.

In an interview with "Boerse Online" magazine published Tuesday, Kuebacher said the single currency might have to be delayed because he saw little chance that Germany would be able to reduce its government deficit enough to meet the key condition for joining European Economic and Monetary Union -- a budget shortfall no larger than 3.0 percent of national output.
A delay in EMU would mean the mark would retain its position as Europe's dominant currency.

On Monday, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel sparked a rush into marks when he told Germany's Bild newspaper that strict adherence to the fiscal criteria for participating in the single currency was more important than the timetable.

Edgar Meister, another Bundesbank member, also sounded an uncompromising tone Monday, saying the success of Europe's common currency largely depended on a stability-oriented interpretation of the various entry criteria.
The yen jumped after Japan's Ministry of Finance announced plans would be drawn up to aid Japan's troubled financial institutions by helping them dispose of bad loans secured by real estate.

"If that comes true, then that only helps the Japanese economy, which, in turn, helps the Nikkei (225 stock index) rally and, in turn, the yen will strengthen," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd.
Britain's currency took the brunt of the mark's surge Tuesday, as talk of EMU delay seemed to undermine its role as a haven from nervousness about forging one currency on the continent.
The U.K. unit was also pressured as the market continued to trim positions in preparation for a general election, which Prime Minister John Major said Monday would take place May 1.

"It's not political jitters associated with the election so much, but I think it's more if there is going to be a delay in EMU, and obviously that has been one of the primary concerns of the market, then sterling as an alternative to EMU is not necessarily needed," said Bob Lynch, senior currency analyst at MMS International, a market consulting firm.
But the pound rose slightly to $1.5900 compared with $1.5887 Monday. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3735 from C$1.3700.
